<reason>B framed the debate correctly from the start: both sides end permanent plots, so the motion lives or dies on mandating composting/hydrolysis specifically. A never defended that mandate squarely. A's "narrow accommodations" (A2.3) ballooned by Rebuttal 2 into time-limited burial, ossuaries, niches, and private-cemetery transfers — which B convincingly read as CON's own program plus optional extras and an escape hatch that resurrects the inequity A's opening condemned. B also turned A's showcase cities against it, corrected A's shaky "fresh fields" mechanics (rotation reuses the same parcel), honestly forced A to admit no municipal-scale operation exists, and punished the "repealed in an afternoon" overconfidence. A had a real, never-fully-killed land argument (rotation locks acres as cemetery forever) and its prose was elegant, but its closing restated that frame without answering the collapse critique, while B's closing documented the retreat with pinpoint references and a clean dilemma: unenforced mandate = slogan, enforced mandate = coercion. A's Q2 exposed that B's rotation also squeezes religious families, a point B partially dodged — that keeps the margin solid rather than dominant.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 1 into Rebuttal 2 sequence on "narrow accommodations": first converting it into a coercion-or-theology-grading dilemma, then, after A4.3's expanded menu, landing "That is my program — plus an escape hatch," which A never answered through the closing.</best_rebuttal>
